read.sections.0.heading.back: A house is more than rooms

read.sections.0.text.note: Nanggala = นังกาลา (no usual Thai name). granaries = ยุ้งข้าว. South Sulawesi as จังหวัดสุลาเวสีใต้ (it is a province).
read.sections.0.text.source:
A house is a place to live, but its design can also express how people are related to each other. Rooms, materials and decoration may reflect work, family ties, beliefs and the resources people had. A photograph shows some features. To understand what they mean, we also need to know about the people and the particular building.

In South Sulawesi, Indonesia, tongkonan are ancestral houses linked with Toraja communities. Ancestral means connected with earlier generations of a family or community. Raised floors, timber frames and curved roofs make these houses easy to recognise. Yet each house belongs to a larger setting. Indonesia's description of traditional Toraja villages includes houses, granaries (rice stores), farmland and places for the community and its ceremonies. Each village keeps its own mix of these. No single village is repeated everywhere.

This is a highland setting on Sulawesi. It is a different island from Java, where the batiks in Lesson 2 were made. Village life joined rice fields and granaries with spaces for family gatherings and ceremonies. At Nanggala, houses and granaries face each other across an open space where people gather. This shows why a roof alone is not the whole architecture. Architecture is the design and building of places. The way buildings stand together also helps organise a community's life. A Toraja example should not stand for all housing in Indonesia.
read.sections.0.text.back:
A house is a place to live, but its design can also tell how people are related to each other. Rooms, materials and decoration can reflect work, family ties, beliefs and the resources people have. A photograph shows some features, but to understand what they mean we need to know the people and that building too.

In South Sulawesi province, Indonesia, a tongkonan is an ancestral house bound up with Toraja communities. The word “ancestral” means connected with earlier generations of a family or community. These houses are easy to recognise because they are raised high, have wooden frames and curved roofs. But each house is part of a larger setting. An Indonesian document describing traditional Toraja villages mentions houses, rice barns (places to store rice), rice fields and spaces for the community and its ceremonies. Each village has its own mix of these; there is no single village type repeated everywhere.

This is the highlands of Sulawesi, a different island from Java, where the batik in Lesson 2 was made. Village life connects rice fields and rice barns with spaces for family gatherings and ceremonies. At Nanggala, houses and rice barns face each other with an open yard in the middle where people gather. This shows why a roof alone is not all of architecture. Architecture is designing and building places. The way buildings stand together also helps organise community life. The Toraja example should not stand for all homes in Indonesia.

read.sections.1.text.note: customary = ตามธรรมเนียม (not in KEY_TERMS; จารีตประเพณี is more formal); used the same way in AAS10. social rank = ฐานะทางสังคม.
read.sections.1.text.source:
Indonesia's national museum, the Museum Nasional Indonesia, explains that a tongkonan is linked with family talks and customary affairs. These are matters guided by a community's long-standing rules. The museum describes three parts: the area below the floor, the main living space and the roof. Each part can carry meaning as well as having a practical use. So architecture organises social life, not just empty space inside walls.

Carving also matters. The museum describes carved walls, doors, windows and roof supports. It explains that some motifs, or repeated designs, are linked to social rank and customary rules. Ornament here is decoration that can also carry meaning. It would be wrong to think that every design is only decoration, or that every house may use every motif. We can describe a carved pattern from a photograph. But we should not invent its meaning because it looks like something we know. Family ties and differences in rank matter to the explanation.
read.sections.1.text.back:
Indonesia's national museum, Museum Nasional Indonesia, explains that a tongkonan is bound up with family discussions and customary matters, matters a community handles by long-held rules. The museum describes the house as having three parts: the space under the floor, the main living space, and the roof. Each part has a practical use and can have meaning too. So architecture organises social life; it is not just empty space inside walls.

Carving matters too. The museum describes carved walls, doors, windows and roof supports, and explains that some motifs, or repeated patterns, are connected with social status and customary rules. Ornament here is decoration that can also carry meaning. Thinking every pattern is just decoration, or that every house may use every motif, is a misunderstanding. We can describe carvings from a photograph, but should not make up meanings just because a pattern looks like something we know. Family ties and differences in status matter to the explanation.

read.sections.1.simpler.source:
Indonesia's national museum says a tongkonan is linked to family talks. It is also linked to customary matters. These are things the group decides by its old rules. The museum names three parts. There is the space under the floor, the main room and the roof. Each part has a use, and it can have a meaning too. So a house helps shape how people live together.

Carving matters too. Walls, doors, windows and roof posts are carved. The museum says some designs are linked to a family's rank. They also follow the group's rules. This kind of ornament is decoration with a meaning. Not every house may use every design. We can describe a carved pattern from a photo. But we should not guess its meaning. It may only look like something we know.
read.sections.1.simpler.back:
Indonesia's national museum says a tongkonan is connected with family discussions, and also with customary matters, matters a group decides by its old rules. The museum says the house has three parts: the space under the floor, the main room and the roof. Each part has a use and can have meaning too. So the house helps decide how people live together.

Carving matters too. Walls, doors, windows and roof posts have carved patterns. The museum says some patterns are connected with a family's status and also follow the group's rules. Ornament like this is decoration with meaning. Not every house can use every pattern. We can describe carvings from a photograph, but should not guess their meaning. A pattern may just look like something we know.

read.sections.2.heading.source: Particular buildings and a living heritage

read.sections.2.text.source:
The two photographs show particular buildings in the Toraja region at particular times. They let us see roofs, repeated shapes and the posts and beams that form each building's structure. We can also see how the buildings stand in relation to each other. But the photographs do not tell us who lived in each room, or what all Toraja people believe today. An ancestral house can matter to many people without being a full picture of family life today.

Heritage is living. People look after buildings, replace materials, change spaces and decide how traditions continue. Living heritage means places and ways of life that people inherit and still use and change. The 2009 submission about the villages describes places that had already changed, not a landscape kept outside history. Studying a tongkonan connects architecture with skilled work, land, family knowledge and earlier generations. It also shows something useful. A building's importance can reach beyond whoever lives in it, because other people see their own connections in the place.
read.sections.2.text.back:
These two photographs show some buildings in Toraja lands at particular moments. They help us see the roofs, repeated shapes, and the posts and beams that are each building's structure. We also see how buildings stand in relation to each other. But a photograph does not tell who lives in which room, or what all Toraja people believe today. Ancestral houses can matter to many people without being a complete picture of family life today.

Heritage is still alive. People look after buildings, replace materials, adapt spaces and decide how traditions will continue. Living heritage means places and ways of life that people have inherited and still use and change. The 2009 proposal document about these villages describes places that have already changed, not a landscape kept outside history. Studying the tongkonan connects architecture with craft, land, family knowledge and earlier generations. It also shows something useful: a building's importance can reach beyond the people living in it, because others also see their own connection to the place.

read.sections.2.simpler.source:
The two photos show some buildings at certain times. We can see roofs, posts and shapes that repeat. The posts and frame are the structure that holds a house up. We can see how the houses stand together. But the photos do not show who lived in each room. They do not show what all Toraja people believe today.

This is living heritage. People still use these places, and they change them. They fix the houses and put in new parts. They decide how the old ways go on. A report from 2009 says the villages had already changed. A tongkonan links building skills, land, family and people of the past. It can matter to many people. It is not only for the people who live in it.
read.sections.2.simpler.back:
These two photographs show some buildings at certain times. We see roofs, posts and repeated shapes. The posts and wooden frame are the structure that keeps the house standing. We see how houses stand together. But the pictures don't tell who lives in which room, and don't tell what all Toraja people believe today.

This is living heritage. People still use these places and change them. They repair houses and put in new parts. They decide how old ways will continue. A 2009 report says the villages have already changed. The tongkonan joins building skills, land, family and people of the past. This house matters to many people, not only to those who live in it.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: Tongkonan are linked with family, customary affairs and ceremonies that communities still keep. Teach them as a community's living practice. No learner is asked to share their own beliefs, family or identity, or to take part in any practice.
sensitiveNotes.0.back: The tongkonan is bound up with family, customary matters and ceremonies the community still practises. Teach this as a community's living practice. No learner is asked to tell about their own beliefs, family or identity, or to take part in any practice.

educatorNotes.0.source: A traditional building is not proof that everyone in a region lives the same way, or that their culture has stopped changing. A Toraja example does not stand for all housing in Indonesia. Keep the pattern a learner can see apart from what a source says it means, and don't invent meanings for carved motifs.
educatorNotes.0.back: Traditional buildings don't prove that everyone in a region lives the same way or that their culture has stopped changing. The Toraja example doesn't stand for all homes in Indonesia. Separate patterns learners can see from meanings sources give, and don't make up meanings of carved motifs.

educatorNotes.1.source: Answer points for Write: an ancestral or family link, family discussion and customary affairs, or carving linked to social standing, connected to a feature a learner can see; the learner keeps the visible pattern apart from the museum's interpretation. Don't require a particular religious belief, or assume all houses today are used the same way.
educatorNotes.1.back: Answer points for the Write step: a connection with ancestors or family, family discussions and customary matters, or carving connected with social status, linked to a feature learners can see; and the learner separates the visible pattern from the museum's interpretation.
